samples.task_summary: Predicting whether an accident is severe in a way that should generalize across shifting environments by favoring stable contextual signals over spurious shortcuts.

scores.rationale: Accident extent can correlate with severity, but it is partly outcome-adjacent and may be noisy or post hoc.
Temperature is a stable weather signal that can affect driving conditions and accident severity.
Humidity is a general weather context variable with some stable relation to conditions, though weaker than direct hazard signals.
Pressure is only indirectly related to weather and is usually a weak predictor on its own.
Low visibility is a strong, semantically meaningful hazard signal that should transfer well across domains.
Wind speed can reflect adverse weather and driving difficulty, but its effect is usually moderate.
Precipitation is a direct and stable indicator of hazardous road conditions.
Nearby amenities are map-context proxies that may capture location type more than severity and can be brittle.
Road bumps are rare and highly local infrastructure cues with limited stable predictive value.
Crossings can matter for traffic complexity, but they are also location-specific and only mildly informative.
Give-way signs are sparse and mostly encode local road design rather than a robust severity signal.
Junctions are a plausible stable risk factor because intersections often increase conflict complexity.
No-exit roads are rare and likely too specific to be broadly useful.
Railway proximity is uncommon and mostly a local geography cue with limited generalization.
Roundabouts may affect traffic patterns, but they are sparse and not a strong universal predictor.
Stations indicate urban/transit context, which can correlate with severity but is a location shortcut.
Stop signs reflect intersection control and can be mildly informative about road complexity.
Traffic calming features are rare and highly local, so they are weak and potentially brittle.
Traffic signals are a meaningful intersection-control cue and can generalize better than many map artifacts.
Year can capture temporal drift, but it is not a causal severity feature and may overfit dataset shifts.
Month captures seasonality in weather and traffic patterns, giving moderate stable signal.
Weekday can reflect commuting and traffic patterns, but the effect is modest and context-dependent.
Day of month is usually a weak calendar artifact with little stable semantic meaning.
Hour is a useful proxy for traffic density and lighting conditions, with reasonably stable predictive value.
Minute is essentially a timestamp artifact and unlikely to generalize meaningfully.
Wind direction can help characterize weather, but it is usually weaker and less directly tied to severity.
Weather condition is a direct hazard descriptor and likely one of the most stable predictors.
Night versus day affects visibility and driving risk, making it a broadly useful temporal context feature.
